newsitem.title: GERMANY: German bourse well-armed to face future challenges.
newsitem.headline: German bourse well-armed to face future challenges.

text.p: Germany's stock exchange said on Monday it is well-armed with innovative new products and ready to do battle with its European counterparts, as competition hots up for international funds.

"Three things -- the products we offer, our prices and our members -- mean that we can expand our current position as leading services provider in all areas of securities," said Werner Seifert, management board chairman of the bourse operating group Deutsche Boerse.
Speaking at the group's annual news conference, Seifert said its portfolio was becoming more focused and the group more service-oriented.
The group's Remote Membership scheme, which allows access to the bourse to market players in other countries, would continue to expand.
"Our cooperation scheme with the Swiss stock exchange will form the nucleus of the European futures exchange EUREX," Seifert said.
"Our cooperation with the Chicago Board Options Exchange and the Options Clearing Corporation in Chicago will set the standard for the trading and clearing of derivative products," he said.

A long-running dispute with Germany's regional bourses over nation-wide cooperation was over, he said. All eight will take part in a new national link-up from July 1, which is aimed at harmonising prices at the eight German bourses.
Smaller stock exchanges in Stuttgart, Hanover, Hamburg and Bremen will join their larger counterparts in Frankfurt, Munich, Berlin and Duesseldorf in the pact.

Seifert said the cooperation pact "embodies the principle of one price per security at the same time" and would remove the "embarrassing price differences" between the regional bourses which have led to arbitrage on shares quoted on more than one exchange.
Arbitrage is where dealers exploit market imperfections, such as the existence of different prices for the same security, to trade securities at a profit.

Earlier attempts by the exchanges to cooperate have foundered on the fears of the smaller stock exchanges that they would as a result lose business and influence to the powerful shadow of the Frankfurt bourse.
Stuttgart, Hanover, Hamburg and Bremen appealed to the cartel authorities late last year to ensure their competitive positions were not in danger.

The group was also upbeat on its fledgling "New Market" scheme, saying that 20 companies were still expected to list on the new exchange for growth stocks in its first year, although only two have listed so far.
New Market, modelled on New York's NASDAQ exchange, had got off to a "fulsome start" in terms of share prices and liquidity since its March 10 launch, board member Reto Francioni said.

Thus far only mobile telephone services firm MobilCom and engineering services group Bertrandt have opted to list on the New Market, which is mainly aimed at innovation stocks, but Francioni said more were coming soon.

"We will see announcements from a number of companies planning to list on the New Market segment in coming weeks," Francioni said, but the next flotation would only take place in three or four months.
Francioni would not be drawn on the names of companies planning to list or say what sectors they come from.
New Market was set up in March amid hopes that it would breathe new life into Germany's cautious investment world.

It was developed and is promoted by Deutsche Boerse and is designed to encourage innovative young firms to tap into a small but growing demand in Germany for potentially high-yielding, risk-bearing investments.
